kind: lemma
title: Pooled-mixture projection and variance
status: draft
origin: pipeline

      url: "https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/dp187pj2131/dp187pj2131_2011-09.pdf"

## Statement

Use the setup of [[def-two-sample-order-r-u-statistic-and-first-projections]]
and suppose $h$ is antisymmetric under exchange of its two blocks and has finite second moment under every independent P/Q assignment to its $2r$ positions. For
$t\in(0,1)$ put $\bar P_t=tP+(1-t)Q$ and define

$$g_t(z)=\int h(z,z_2,\ldots,z_r;w_1,\ldots,w_r)\,d\bar P_t^{\otimes(2r-1)}-\theta(\bar P_t,\bar P_t;h).$$

Then $\theta(\bar P_t,\bar P_t;h)=0$, the first projection in the second block
is $-g_t$, and $\sigma_t^2:=E_{\bar P_t}[g_t^2]$ is finite. The map $t\mapsto\sigma_t^2$ is continuous on
$(0,1)$. In particular, for $p_N=m/N\to p\in(0,1)$,

$$r^2\left(1+\frac{m}{n}\right)\sigma_{p_N}^2\longrightarrow\frac{r^2}{1-p}\sigma_p^2.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A block-symmetric kernel, its antisymmetry under exchange of blocks, and finite second moments under all mixed P/Q assignments.

[F1] [[def-two-sample-order-r-u-statistic-and-first-projections]] defines the block kernel and its first projections.

[F2] [[lem-two-sample-u-statistic-projections-well-defined]] gives the section-integral versions and their L2 bounds.

[F3] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] defines the second-moment variance $E[g_t^2]$ when $E g_t=0$.

[F4] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] makes cross products of the finitely many square-integrable mixed-assignment section functions integrable.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement. Prove the pooled mean, sign relation, finiteness, and continuity claims.

1.1 Under $\bar P_t^{\otimes 2r}$, swapping the first and second blocks preserves the product law and changes $h$ to $-h$. Therefore $\theta(\bar P_t,\bar P_t;h)=-\theta(\bar P_t,\bar P_t;h)$, so it is zero. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Expand each factor $\bar P_t=tP+(1-t)Q$ in the section integral. This writes $g_t$ as a finite sum $\sum_\eta c_\eta(t)f_\eta(z)$, where $\eta$ ranges over assignments of P and Q to the remaining $2r-1$ coordinates, $c_\eta(t)$ is a polynomial, and $f_\eta$ is the corresponding section integral. For either first-coordinate law $R\in\{P,Q\}$, write $E_{R,\eta}$ for product expectation with independent coordinates having law $R$ first and the laws specified by $\eta$ in the remaining positions. The mixed-moment assumption gives both $E_{P,\eta}[h^2]<\infty$ and $E_{Q,\eta}[h^2]<\infty$. Fubini applied with first-coordinate law $(P+Q)/2$ supplies one measurable version of $f_\eta$, valid $(P+Q)$-almost everywhere after setting it to zero on the common exceptional set. Cauchy--Schwarz on the remaining probability product then gives $\int |f_\eta|^2\,dR\le E_{R,\eta}[h^2]<\infty$ for each $R\in\{P,Q\}$, as in the section-integral argument of [F2]. Consequently every cross integral $\int f_\eta f_{\eta'}\,dR$ is finite by [F4]. Expanding $E_{\bar P_t}g_t^2=tE_P[g_t^2]+(1-t)E_Q[g_t^2]$ now gives a finite sum of polynomial coefficients times these finite cross integrals, so it is finite and continuous in $t$. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Integrating the first coordinate of $h$ while the other $2r-1$ coordinates have law $\bar P_t$ defines $g_t$, since its mean in [F1] is zero by step 1.1. For the projection in the second block, exchange the blocks inside the integral. Antisymmetry changes the sign and the common product law is unchanged, so the second-block projection is $-g_t$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $m/n=p_N/(1-p_N)$ and $p_N\to p$, step 1.2 gives $\sigma_{p_N}^2\to\sigma_p^2$, while $1+m/n=1/(1-p_N)\to1/(1-p)$. Multiplication by $r^2$ proves the displayed limit. [step 1.2, algebra] ∎
rows.current_focused_review: Focused current review confirms the added all-independent-P/Q-assignment finite-second-moment hypothesis is now in the opening Statement. For each of the finitely many section functions f_eta, sectionwise Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its squared integral under either first-coordinate law by the corresponding mixed kernel moment; the common (P+Q)-null-set prescription supplies simultaneous versions. Expanding g_t and then E_(tP+(1-t)Q)[g_t^2] gives finite polynomial coefficients times finite cross-integrals, proving the stated finiteness and continuity. Antisymmetry gives the zero pooled parameter and opposite projections. The old claim genuinely failed: for P=delta_0, Q density 3x^-4 on [1,infinity), h(x,y)=xy(x-y), its direct P-times-Q moment is zero but the pooled first projection mu_t*z^2-nu_t*z has infinite second moment because mu_t>0 and EQ^4=infinity. The native fatal classification and fixed disposition are therefore retained.

      url: "https://static.renyi.hu/~major/articles/lect-note1.pdf"
    - title: "E. Y. Chung and J. P. Romano, Asymptotically Valid and Exact Permutation Tests Based on Two-Sample U-Statistics, Stanford Technical Report 2011-09, §3.2"
      url: "https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/dp187pj2131/dp187pj2131_2011-09.pdf"
---

## Statement

In the setup of [[def-two-sample-order-r-u-statistic-and-first-projections]],
assume $h\in L^2(P^{\otimes r}\otimes Q^{\otimes r})$. For each $X$-coordinate
$u$ let $P_u$ integrate that coordinate under $P$; for each $Y$-coordinate
let $P_u$ integrate under $Q$, and put $Q_u=I-P_u$. These coordinate
operators commute on $h$ by Fubini. For $0\le a,b\le r$, choose any $a$ of
the $X$-coordinates and any $b$ of the $Y$-coordinates, apply $Q_u$ in those
coordinates and $P_u$ in all others, and call the resulting (reindexed)
kernel $h_{a,b}$. Separate block symmetry makes it independent of the chosen
coordinate subsets. It is canonical in each of its $a+b$ arguments: integrating
it in any such argument gives zero. Let $U_{a,b}(h_{a,b})$ be its average over
all $a$-subsets of the $X$ sample and all $b$-subsets of the $Y$ sample, with
the zero-order convention $U_{0,0}=\theta(P,Q;h)$. Then

$$U_{m,n}-\theta(P,Q;h)=\sum_{\substack{0\le a,b\le r\\a+b\ge1}}\binom ra\binom rb\,U_{a,b}(h_{a,b}).$$

In particular,

$$U_{m,n}-\theta(P,Q;h)=\frac r m\sum_{i=1}^m g_X(X_i)+\frac r n\sum_{j=1}^n g_Y(Y_j)+R_{m,n},$$

where $R_{m,n}$ is the sum of the terms with $a+b\ge2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent IID samples from $P$ and $Q$, a symmetric order-$(r,r)$ kernel with finite second moment, and the projection definitions.

[F1] [[def-two-sample-order-r-u-statistic-and-first-projections]] defines $U_{m,n}$, $g_X$, and $g_Y$.

[F2] [[lem-two-sample-u-statistic-projections-well-defined]] supplies measurable square-integrable coordinate integrals and the Fubini equalities needed for each projection operator.

[F3] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] permits the coordinate-integration operators on different coordinates to commute.

[F4] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives the $L^2$ contraction bound for integration over a probability coordinate.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement. Prove the finite decomposition and identify its order-one terms.

1.1 For each coordinate $u$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] on its probability marginal and Fubini [F3] give $\|P_uh\|_2\le\|h\|_2$. The pointwise inequality $|h-P_uh|^2\le2|h|^2+2|P_uh|^2$ then gives $\|Q_uh\|_2\le2\|h\|_2$. Thus every finite product of the coordinate operators is a well-defined $L^2$ class. The operator $P_u$ is idempotent because integrating an already coordinate-independent function changes nothing. For distinct coordinates $u,v$, Fubini [F3] gives $P_uP_v=P_vP_u$ on each integrable section, so $P_u,Q_u$ commute across distinct coordinates. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Since $I=P_u+Q_u$ for every one of the $2r$ coordinates, multiplying these finitely many identities and using commutativity expands $h$ as the sum over all subsets of coordinates of the corresponding products of $P_u$ and $Q_u$. This is a finite algebraic expansion; its empty selected subset is $P_1\cdots P_{2r}h=\theta(P,Q;h)$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If coordinate $u$ is selected, applying $P_u$ to that component gives zero because $P_uQ_u=P_u-P_u^2=0$; the other commuting factors do not alter this identity. Thus each component is canonical in each selected coordinate. Block symmetry identifies the $\binom ra\binom rb$ components with $a$ selected $X$-coordinates and $b$ selected $Y$-coordinates as reindexed copies of $h_{a,b}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply the expansion in step 2.1 to each summand $h(X_I;Y_J)$ in $U_{m,n}$, summing over sample subsets and selected kernel coordinates together. Each fixed $a$-subset of the $X$ sample is contained in exactly $\binom{m-a}{r-a}$ sample $r$-subsets; in each, exactly one choice of $a$ kernel coordinates selects it. Thus its coefficient after averaging is $\binom{m-a}{r-a}/\binom mr=\binom ra/\binom ma$. Similarly, each fixed $b$-subset of the $Y$ sample has coefficient $\binom rb/\binom nb$. These identities also hold when $a=0$ or $b=0$. Block symmetry identifies the resulting functions with $h_{a,b}$, so the combined contribution is $\binom ra\binom rb U_{a,b}(h_{a,b})$. Removing the constant component gives the first displayed decomposition. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For $(a,b)=(1,0)$, the integrated kernel is exactly $g_X$ from [F1], and its subset average is $m^{-1}\sum_i g_X(X_i)$; its coefficient is $\binom r1=r$. For $(a,b)=(0,1)$ the average is $n^{-1}\sum_j g_Y(Y_j)$ with the same coefficient $r$. All remaining pairs have $a+b\ge2$ and are, by definition, the remainder $R_{m,n}$. [F1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-two-sample-order-r-u-statistic-and-first-projections]],
$r$ is fixed, $m/N\to p\in(0,1)$, $\theta(P,Q;h)=0$, and
$0<E_P[g_X^2]=\sigma_X^2<\infty$ and
$0<E_Q[g_Y^2]=\sigma_Y^2<\infty$. If the fixed-order kernel has finite
second moments under all mixed assignments, then

$$\sqrt m\,U_{m,n}\Rightarrow N\!\left(0,\ r^2\left(\sigma_X^2+\frac p{1-p}\sigma_Y^2\right)\right).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent IID samples from $P$ and $Q$, fixed $r$, $m/N\to p\in(0,1)$, a zero parameter, and positive finite first-projection variances.

[F1] [[def-two-sample-order-r-u-statistic-and-first-projections]] defines $U_{m,n}$ and its centered projections $g_X,g_Y$.

[F2] [[lem-two-sample-u-statistic-degenerate-remainder-order]] gives $\sqrt N R_{m,n}\to0$ in $L^2$ under the mixed second-moment premises.

[F3] [[thm-lindeberg-levy-iid-central-limit-theorem]]: under AC, each IID centered real sample mean with positive finite variance has its normalized normal limit.

[F4] [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]], [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]], and [[cor-characteristic-function-criterion-for-weak-convergence]] give the independent-sum normal limit.

[F5] [[thm-slutsky-for-real-random-variables]] transfers a weak limit after adding a term converging to zero in probability.

[A1] AC is assumed exactly for the CLT and characteristic-function suppliers in [F3]–[F4]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The assumptions in the Statement. Prove the centered normal limit at scale $\sqrt m$.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $\sqrt m\,U_{m,n}=r\frac1{\sqrt m}\sum_{i=1}^m g_X(X_i)+r\sqrt{\frac mn}\left(\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^n g_Y(Y_j)\right)+\sqrt m R_{m,n},$ and the final term tends to zero in probability because $m/N$ is bounded and $E[(\sqrt N R_{m,n})^2]\to0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 The summands $g_X(X_i)$ are IID, centered, and have variance $\sigma_X^2$; [F3] gives $m^{-1/2}\sum_i g_X(X_i)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_X^2)$. The $g_Y(Y_j)$ are IID, centered, and have variance $\sigma_Y^2$, so the same result gives $n^{-1/2}\sum_j g_Y(Y_j)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2)$. The two sums are independent because the two samples are independent. [F1, F3, A1, given]
